dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer

kp.k: Expert-built environments replace lower-skilled behaviour-cloning data
kp.d: Foody describes a transition, especially heading into 2024, from crowdsourced supervised fine-tuning and preference data toward highly skilled experts collaborating on frontier evaluations and reinforcement-learning environments. Lawyers join software engineers, doctors and bankers as contributors to model development. He reports 2.5 million expert hours in Q2 alone, within a graph covering the preceding 24 months, attributing demand to expanding environments across economic activities.
qs: this giant transition away from the low-skilled crowdsourcing era of behavior cloning data and moving towards the agentic era of data.
All the software engineers, lawyers, doctors, bankers, et cetera that could measure the frontier of intelligence and help to use that to improve model capabilities.
2.5 million hours um, in Q2 alone

kp.k: Environments combine workplace context, applications and scored tasks
kp.d: Foody defines RL environments as worlds containing project materials, high-fidelity application clones and tasks with prompts and verifiers. Rubrics or unit tests can support evaluation or training. He frames coverage of the economy’s different worlds, applications and tasks as a barrier to automating laptop-based work, rather than presenting comprehensive automation as already achieved.
qs: The first part is the worlds. So, this includes all of the messages, slides, docs, sheets, etc. that correspond to everything you would have in a real project or company that you're working on.
The second part is the apps which is high fidelity clones of popular applications, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Microsoft 365, etc.
And then the third part is the tasks where we have prompts and verifiers. Verifiers could be rubrics or unit tests that can be used either for eval or training.

kp.k: Lawyers translate practice experience into simulated legal work
kp.d: Foody’s published legal-environment example uses lawyers from firms such as Latham and Watkins to reconstruct scenarios from their work and outline extensive data rooms. Models help populate these materials, which are rendered into cloned applications. The illustrated task assesses comparative maximum liability using the data-room context. This describes lawyers creating training and evaluation infrastructure, not evidence of autonomous performance on live client matters.
qs: we have lawyers from top law firms like Latham and Watkins write out a scenario of a real project that they worked on in their big law job.
And then they create a full outline for a data room that corresponds to all of the different uh messages, emails, files, size of files.
and then we render that data room into the apps, the clones of Google Workspace you can see in this scenario, and have prompts uh to roll out model trajectories against this.

kp.k: Human expertise supplies signals beyond models’ existing capabilities
kp.d: Foody argues that models cannot reliably identify their own errors in most open-ended domains, including legal environments and legal memos. Experts are therefore especially important for task creation and rubric design, although AI copilots can increase their efficiency. He qualifies this argument with exceptions involving clean mathematical feedback, code, cybersecurity and stronger models teaching weaker ones. These verifiers score training outputs; the discussion is not a claim about professional verification of advice before client reliance.
qs: Only humans can measure the frontier in most domains, not every domain.
Like the models you you can't just tell the model like come up with the legal environment and then like tell me which of your legal memos are like good and bad.
We have found that you can make it a lot more efficient if you have a like AI copilot that's able to work with the expert in creating the task and the verifier.
the process that requires humans the most is the task creation.

kp.k: Data quality requires realism and reliable trajectory scoring
kp.d: Foody identifies two dimensions of quality: realistic coverage of workplace activities and accurate verifiers. For corporate law, expert outlines and taxonomies are intended to reflect the distribution of real legal environments. Rubrics must accommodate multiple valid solutions and mistakes while resisting reward hacking. He describes trajectory analysis using 10 model trajectories, automated quality-control systems and human review, with human preferences potentially evaluating the automatic grader.

what we do for that is a process called trajectory analysis, where we roll out 10 trajectories of the model that we're focused on improving

kp.k: Reported post-training gains include corporate-law benchmark improvement
kp.d: Foody reports an Apex Agents post-training example with 1,800 tasks and about 500k in compute, in which corporate-law performance rose from 4.7% to 26.6%. He also claims generalisation to other evaluations, including Apex V1 without data rooms, and nominal gains on some other benchmarks. These are speaker-reported model-evaluation results, not measured legal-service outcomes. The transcript identifies the trained model as “GLM 47” but explicitly warns that proper nouns are unreliable.

This was post-training run of GLM 47

kp.k: Domain-specific intelligence becomes an application-company competitive strategy
kp.d: Foody describes compute, algorithms or researchers, and datasets as core AI-strategy components, with data often the most differentiating. He says Mercor works with Harvey to construct domain-specific environments. Using Cursor as a precedent, he predicts dozens of application companies will own their own intelligence over the next 12 months. This is his strategic forecast, not evidence that those future models or competitive advantages already exist.
qs: the three core pillars of their AI strategy are their compute, their algorithms or researchers, and the data sets they build. And data's often the most differentiating factor.

working with customers like Harvey, who I know will present on stuff later to help build out the environments corresponding to their specific domain so that they can build frontier intelligence within that.
I believe that over the next 12 months, there is going to be dozens of examples just like that where companies own their own intelligence

kp.k: Expert labour is packaged into scalable data products
kp.d: Foody distinguishes custom per-task datasets, off-the-shelf datasets sold to multiple customers and hourly provision of experts. He says Harvey initially hired lawyers through Mercor, but engagements generally move toward scaled data offerings. Illustrations include $2,000 per legal-environment task, certain frontier labs buying 50,000 tasks monthly, and tasks requiring a few hours to as much as a month of human work. These prices concern AI-training inputs, not fees charged for client legal services.
qs: I really like this data shape of environments in law and we will pay $2,000 per task to scale this up.
certain frontier labs might buy 50,000 tasks a month from us.
Some would even take humans up to a month to complete that given task. Sometimes it would take just a few hours.
we've invested hundreds of millions of dollars in building our own data sets that we sell to multiple customers.
that was how Harvey got started with us hiring uh some lawyers

kp.k: Training-data prices reflect improvement value and production costs
kp.d: Foody says pricing works backward from customers’ desired model improvement and leaderboard goals, while also accounting for expert-production costs and differentiation. He gives an illustrative cost basis of $1500 for 10 hours at $150 an hour and reports task prices ranging from $50 to $10,000. His example of Nvidia potentially paying a billion dollars for a frontier open-source model is explicitly hypothetical willingness to pay.

we're able to work backwards from how much is that worth to them and how much should we charge uh per task, how many tasks do we think would get them to that goal.
when we have a task that takes 10 hours of human time and we're paying the human $150 an hour there might be a $1500 cost basis
we have tasks that range from $50 to $10,000.

kp.k: Synthetic generation complements rather than eliminates expert contribution
kp.d: Foody distinguishes synthetic model trajectories used for learning from model assistance in populating environments and creating tasks. He characterises RLVR itself as a bet on synthetic data, replacing human-written supervised examples with scored model trajectories. He nevertheless maintains that expert guidance is necessary for realistic environments and dependable judgments beyond a model’s capability frontier.
qs: RLVR is a bet on synthetic data.
let's roll out a bunch of synthetic model trajectories rather than having the humans write the SFT, and then let's score all of them
models play giant role in the way that we populate environments and create tasks
you need humans almost definitionally to measure what is beyond the frontier of the model capabilities.

kp.k: Long-horizon work and social interaction remain development priorities
kp.d: Foody attributes the expansion of application-rich environments in 2025 to bottlenecks in using workplace context and tools. Looking forward, he proposes tasks corresponding to 100 or 1,000 human hours, against his claim that agents mostly are not trained for work exceeding 10 hours. He also calls for virtual co-workers: informal responses suggesting 60% or 70% of work involves other people contrast with his estimate that about 1% of evaluations measures such interaction. These figures are presented as illustrative observations, not a documented workforce study.
qs: right now agents mostly aren't trained to do things that are over 10 hours, and we need to start building tasks for things that might take a human 100 hours or even 1,000 hours to do.
the other large shift that we're seeing is introducing virtual co-workers
most people would say like 60% or 70%.
what percentage of evals measure how well the models can interact with other people, it's like 1%, maybe Tau bench has a little bit of this.
there's this giant realism gap associated with how you actually measure how well agents engage in social interaction

kp.k: Occasional task success indicates a model’s training potential
kp.d: Asked about base-model limitations, Foody acknowledges parameter count but recommends comparing pass-at-one with pass-at-16. A model that fails once but succeeds on one or two of 16 trajectories offers useful learning opportunities; repeated total failure suggests that the dataset may be beyond its effective learning capability. He presents this as a heuristic, with the qualification that additional attempts might uncover a successful trajectory.
qs: the parameter count will definitely play a role in how effectively the model does insofar as how trainable it is.
the main thing to look at is generally the gap between the like pass at 16 and the pass at one.
pass at one it fails, but then pass at 16 when you roll out 16 trajectories it gets it right once or twice, and then the model is able to learn very effectively from that.

kp.k: Exclusive custom datasets coexist with shared supplier infrastructure
kp.d: Foody argues that customers can preserve competitive advantage through owned datasets and siloed, exclusive teams while relying on Mercor’s common infrastructure and expert network. He contrasts this arrangement with building talent networks and infrastructure internally, attributing the partnership model’s appeal to economies of scale. This is the supplier’s argument about AI-development organisation, rather than independent evidence of superior outsourcing outcomes.
qs: we have teams that are siloed and fully exclusive to critical customers to make sure that we build out the best data sets in the world that they own.
that allows them to maintain their competitive advantage associated with this, while also benefiting from all of the infrastructure that we've built.
there are some companies that try to like build out all of the talent network and infrastructure in-house

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Brendan Foody claims that expert-built reinforcement-learning environments improve agents' ability to perform realistic professional work, including corporate-law tasks, and enable application companies such as Harvey to develop domain-specific intelligence.
pts.d: Foody describes environments combining realistic project documents, application clones and tasks scored by rubrics or tests. His legal example uses lawyers from top firms to reconstruct a project scenario and data room, against which an agent performs a liability analysis. He reports improved corporate-law benchmark performance after post-training and generalisation to other benchmarks. These are claims about training and measured model capabilities, not demonstrated replacement of lawyers or measured improvements in client outcomes. He frames comprehensive automation of laptop-based work, including corporate law, as an ambition constrained by coverage of real tasks, tools and contexts.

pts.k: Foody predicts that proprietary intelligence and differentiated training data will become major competitive advantages for application-layer AI companies.
pts.d: He predicts dozens of companies will follow the example he attributes to Cursor within the following 12 months. He identifies compute, algorithms or researchers, and datasets as the core pillars of AI strategy, with data often the most differentiating. He argues that exclusive custom datasets allow customers to retain competitive advantage while benefiting from a specialist supplier's infrastructure and talent network. This is a cross-domain market prediction that explicitly includes Harvey as a customer; it is not a claim that Harvey itself delivers legal services as an ALSP.

pts.k: Foody claims AI changes expert work rather than eliminating the need for experts in frontier training: models assist production, while humans remain essential for realistic tasks and reliable assessment beyond model capabilities.
pts.d: He describes a transition from low-skilled preference labelling and behaviour-cloning data to teams of highly skilled professionals creating evaluations and RL environments. He recommends that lawyers use Claude or ChatGPT for memo drafting and that experts use models to populate data rooms and assist rubric construction. He nevertheless claims a frontier model cannot reliably identify and score its own errors in many professional domains. His references to 'verifiers' concern training or evaluation scoring mechanisms, not human verification of legal advice before client reliance. He offers exceptions for cleanly testable domains and training weaker models using stronger ones.

pts.k: Foody forecasts a shift toward training agents on much longer projects and interactions with virtual co-workers.
pts.d: Across professional work, he identifies inadequate training on long-horizon tasks and social interaction as gaps between existing evaluations and real jobs. He anticipates tasks equivalent to 100 or 1,000 hours of human work and environments incorporating virtual colleagues. This is a proposed direction of training development, not a claim that agents already autonomously complete projects of that duration.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal quantitative evidence offered is a Mercor post-training example; other support comes from Foody's descriptions of customer work, expert hours and training-quality processes.
pts.d: Foody reports an Apex Agents run using 1,800 tasks and approximately 500k in compute, with corporate-law performance increasing from 4.7% to 26.6%. He also reports generalisation to other benchmarks without supplying their scores in the transcript. The transcript does not define the corporate-law metric, provide a full experimental protocol or establish independent validation. Model and benchmark names in the captions are unreliable, so their rendered spellings should not be treated as confirmed identifiers. He cites 2.5 million expert hours in Q2 as evidence of scaling demand for environment construction. His operational examples include a published legal environment, work with Harvey and trajectory analysis comparing rubric scores with human judgments. The competitive-moat prediction relies on company experience and analogy to Cursor rather than a presented forecast model. His social-interaction percentages are informal estimates based on questions he asks people, not a described systematic study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Foody situates the change in data production around 2024–2025, describes current results at the supplied August 2026 session date, and gives a 12-month horizon for proprietary application-model proliferation.
pts.d: He places the move toward highly skilled agentic data work around 2024 and the growth of application-rich environments in 2025. His 'next 12 months' prediction is relative to the document's stated 12 August 2026 date; the long-horizon and virtual-co-worker shifts have no firm completion date. He conditions effective training on realistic coverage, accurate rubrics resistant to reward hacking and a sufficiently capable base model. He uses the gap between pass-at-one and pass-at-16 as a heuristic: a model must sometimes produce successful trajectories to learn effectively from their rewards. Human dependence is qualified by exceptions in mathematics, code, some cyber tasks and distillation from stronger models. The Q2 expert-hours figure is not explicitly assigned a year in the spoken excerpt.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are expert professionals, legal-AI and other application vendors, frontier labs and specialist training-data suppliers.
pts.d: Lawyers, including those with large-firm experience, supply scenarios, task design and evaluative judgment while using AI to assist production. Harvey is presented as a buyer of expert labour and increasingly scaled domain-specific datasets. Application vendors gain a proposed route to owning differentiated models; frontier labs buy large task collections; Mercor supplies shared infrastructure, datasets and expert teams. Corporate-law work is a target domain for capability development and eventual automation, but Foody gives no quantified prediction of lawyer job losses, staffing changes, legal fees or access-to-justice effects. His examples primarily concern professional and enterprise workflows rather than unmet civil legal need.
